findings.summary: FinCEN assessed a record $1.3 billion civil money penalty against TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank USA, N.A. for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money laundering regulations, including failures to maintain an adequate AML program and to identify and report suspicious activity. The settlement also imposed a four-year independent monitorship.

The OCC issued a cease and desist order, assessed a $450 million civil money penalty, and imposed an asset cap and growth restriction on TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank USA, N.A. for systemic BSA/AML compliance deficiencies, including failures in suspicious activity reporting and currency transaction reporting.

The Federal Reserve Board issued a cease and desist order and assessed a civil money penalty against Toronto-Dominion Bank, TD Group U.S. Holdings, LLC, and TD Bank U.S. Holding Company for BSA/AML compliance failures, in coordination with parallel actions by the OCC, FinCEN, and DOJ.

TD Bank, N.A. pleaded guilty to conspiring to fail to maintain an AML program, fail to file accurate Currency Transaction Reports, and launder monetary instruments. Its parent TD Bank US Holding Company simultaneously pleaded guilty to related charges. As part of the plea agreements, TD Bank will pay a combined $1.8 billion in penalties, remediate its AML program, and retain an independent monitor.

The CFPB issued a consent order against TD Bank, N.A. for violating the Fair Credit Reporting Act and Regulation V by furnishing inaccurate consumer credit and deposit account information and failing to conduct reasonable and timely investigations of disputes. The order requires $7.76 million in redress and a $20 million civil money penalty.

The CFTC issued an order against The Toronto Dominion Bank (TD Bank) for recordkeeping and supervision failures related to firm-wide use of unapproved communication methods, requiring TD Bank to pay a $75 million civil monetary penalty and to cease and desist from further violations.

OFAC settled with TD Bank, N.A. for $115,005.04 over two matters involving apparent violations of the North Korea Sanctions Regulations and the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations, including processing transactions and maintaining accounts for North Korean UN mission employees and a Specially Designated National without a license.

TD Bank pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering and faced US$3.09 billion in monetary penalties from US regulators, with business restrictions and an asset cap on its US retail banking business. Shareholders filed a securities class action (Tiessen v. TD Bank) in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York in October 2024 alleging misrepresentations about TD's AML controls.

In Tiessen v. The Toronto-Dominion Bank, a federal judge on October 13, 2026 largely denied the defendants' motion to dismiss, allowing most securities fraud claims regarding alleged AML misstatements to proceed to discovery in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.

An Ontario class action against Toronto-Dominion Bank alleging misrepresentations about its AML controls had its leave and certification motions heard before the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in February and May 2026, with the matter to conclude by July 23, 2026.

In Burns v. TD Bank, N.A., a class action over APSN overdraft fees, TD Bank agreed to a settlement providing US$32,225,000 in total relief (US$21,975,000 cash and US$10,250,000 in balance reductions), which was paid out in 2025. TD Bank denied wrongdoing.

Trisal v. TD Bank, N.A., a proposed class action filed on October 2, 2025 in the District of New Jersey, alleges TD Bank routinely failed to honor its own overdraft grace period refund policy. Court records list the case as terminated on May 15, 2026, with no settlement or fund.

A Canadian class action over duplicative NSF fees charged by TD Bank on re-presented pre-authorized debits was settled, with the Settlement Agreement approved by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice on February 15, 2024. The settlement distribution has concluded.

A proposed class action against Toronto-Dominion Bank alleging failure to properly pay commissioned Mobile Mortgage Specialists vacation and holiday pay under the Canada Labour Code was certified as a class proceeding by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice on April 10, 2026. TD Bank filed a Notice of Appeal on May 11, 2026.

In In re Toronto-Dominion Bank / First Horizon Corp. Sec. Litig., the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey dismissed plaintiffs' claims on November 26, 2025, on the ground that plaintiffs were not purchasers or sellers of TD Bank securities and lacked standing.

On October 10, 2024, TD Bank N.A. and its parent TD Bank US Holding Company pleaded guilty to conspiring to fail to maintain an adequate anti-money laundering program, fail to file accurate Currency Transaction Reports, and launder monetary instruments. The bank will pay a combined $1.8 billion in penalties, enhance its AML compliance program, and retain an independent monitor—the largest BSA penalty ever imposed and the first guilty plea by a U.S. national bank for money laundering conspiracy.

Following the October 2024 guilty plea, TD Bank received a cease-and-desist order and non-financial sanctions from the OCC, including an asset cap limiting its U.S. growth due to 'significant, systemic breakdowns' in its transaction monitoring program.
On February 27, 2025, TD Bank appointed an independent compliance monitor as required by its plea agreement following the $3 billion U.S. penalty for money laundering.

Wilfredo Aquino, a former TD Bank assistant store manager, pleaded guilty in January 2026 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments. From 2019 to February 2021, he facilitated a money laundering network's movement of approximately $474 million through TD Bank accounts, accepting over $11,000 in retail gift cards as bribes.
On July 16, 2026, former TD Bank assistant store manager Wilfredo Aquino was sentenced to prison for facilitating money laundering and fraud through TD Bank accounts from 2019 to February 2021.

On January 21, 2026, former TD Bank employee Nunez pleaded guilty to facilitating a Colombian ATM money laundering scheme. From March 2021 to October 2023, he accepted bribes and opened fraudulent accounts used to expatriate over $26 million from the U.S. to Colombia via more than 120,000 ATM withdrawals.

On January 30, 2026, former TD Bank employee Leonardo Ayala pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receiving bribes as a bank employee. From June to November 2023, he opened fraudulent accounts and issued over 150 debit cards used to launder approximately $5.5 million to Colombia via more than 12,000 ATM withdrawals, receiving over $6,000 in bribes.

On June 10, 2026, former TD Bank retail banker Leonardo Ayala was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release for accepting bribes and facilitating the laundering of more than $5.5 million to Colombia.

On October 6, 2026, former TD Bank employee Wilfredo Aquino pleaded guilty to a separate two-count information charging him with conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receipt of bribes by a bank employee. From April 2022 to November 2023, he opened 86 fraudulent accounts used to launder approximately $4.8 million to Colombia, receiving over $8,000 in bribes. Sentencing is set for March 23, 2027.

OFAC announced a $115,005.04 settlement with TD Bank, N.A. for apparent violations of the North Korea Sanctions Regulations and the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations. In the first matter, TDBNA processed 1,479 transactions totaling $382,685.38 and maintained nine accounts for employees of the North Korean mission to the UN without a license. In the second matter, TDBNA maintained accounts for a U.S. resident on OFAC's SDN List, resulting in 145 apparent violations. The apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and deemed non-egregious.

On October 10, 2024, TD Bank, N.A. and its parent TD Bank US Holding Company pleaded guilty to conspiring to fail to maintain an AML program under the Bank Secrecy Act, fail to file accurate Currency Transaction Reports, and launder monetary instruments. TD Bank agreed to pay a combined $1.8 billion in penalties, the largest BSA penalty ever imposed by DOJ and the first guilty plea by a U.S. national bank for money laundering conspiracy. The failures enabled three money laundering networks to transfer more than $670 million through TD Bank accounts between 2019 and 2023.

FinCEN assessed a record $1.3 billion civil penalty against TD Bank for willful failures to maintain an adequate AML program and file SARs on thousands of suspicious transactions totaling approximately $1.5 billion. The Consent Order found that TD Bank's monitoring gaps resulted in approximately $18.3 trillion in unmonitored transaction activity, and that the bank failed to address funnel account activity involving high-risk countries. The order also noted that a former TD Bank branch manager was suspected of colluding to circumvent reporting requirements, and that the bank's investigation failed to escalate potential Cuba sanctions issues.

TD Bank, N.A. disclosed a data breach in which an employee accessed and misused customer account information between December 22, 2025 and March 11, 2026 (with UpGuard reporting the window as January 7–30, 2026). Compromised data included names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and transactional data. The bank began notifying affected customers on or around May 26, 2026, and the incident is being investigated by TD Bank's corporate security team.

TD Bank, N.A. notified the New Hampshire Attorney General on October 26, 2026 of a privacy event in which an employee compromised customer personal information on August 27, 2026. Exposed data included names, addresses, email, phone numbers, Social Security numbers, identification numbers, transactional data, dates of birth, and account numbers. The bank offered affected customers two years of free credit monitoring.
TD Bank, N.A. reported a privacy event to the New Hampshire Attorney General on September 28, 2026, identifying 14 New Hampshire customers impacted by an employee-related data breach.

TD Bank reported multiple data breach incidents to the Massachusetts Attorney General in 2026, including one on May 15, 2026 affecting 2 MA residents (with SSN, financial account, and driver's license data breached), one on September 4, 2026 affecting 54 MA residents (financial account data breached), and one on November 20, 2026 affecting 2 MA residents (SSN breached).

Plaintiff Earl Crumpe filed a class action lawsuit (Crumpe v. TD Bank N.A., Case No. 1:25-cv-01566, D.N.J.) on February 28, 2025, alleging TD Bank allowed a former employee unauthorized network access from August to December 2022, compromising customer names, contact information, dates of birth, account numbers, and transactional data. The lawsuit alleges negligence, breach of implied contract, and violations of the FTC Act.

TD Bank accelerated its CEO transition in response to the U.S. AML matter, with Bharat Masrani retiring as Group President and CEO and from the Board on February 1, 2025, replaced by Raymond Chun. Masrani's 2024 total direct compensation was reduced by 89% (from C$13,271,000 in 2023 to C$1,500,000), and 41 executives received variable compensation reductions totaling C$30 million.

TD Bank's compliance failures, including ignoring warning signs and massive transaction-monitoring gaps, led to a roughly $3 billion fine and raised questions about whether whistleblowers helped build the government's case against the bank.
